chapters.html:
Read this first

This book teaches you how to build and sell one small digital product with Claude and ChatGPT, on weekends, without quitting your job and without writing code yourself.

It does not promise income, a first client, or a date by which you will be profitable. Nobody honest can promise that. What it promises is a method — the same one I used to ship murugaaa.in, thedayzero.in and mentell.co.in — and the real numbers from those builds, including the ones that hurt.

Three things to know before you start:

  • Every number in this book is real and dated. If I don't have a real number, I don't make one up.
  • Tools change every month. Features and screens are described as of October 2026. If a button has moved, the method still works — the "Updates" note at the top of the reader tells you what changed.
  • This is not legal, tax or financial advice. When a chapter touches GST, payments or terms, it tells you what to ask a professional.

How each chapter works

Read one chapter per sitting. Every chapter ends with an Action page. Don't move on until you've done it — the book only works if you build while you read.

  • Insight — the one idea from the section worth remembering
  • Mistake I made — what went wrong in my builds and what to do instead
  • Prompt — copy it, replace the [BRACKETS], run it
  • Action page — do this before the next chapter
  • Milestone — something real you can point to

The 12-weekend map

The book follows the order in which you build. One part per stage, one milestone per weekend.

  1. The Shift · Weekend 1
  2. AI Studio · Weekends 2–3
  3. Find and Prove · Weekends 4–5
  4. Build It · Weekends 6–8
  5. Sell It · Weekends 9–11
  6. Improve and Scale · Weekend 12

By the end of Weekend 12 you will have: a validated idea, a live website on your own domain, a working payment link, a product someone can buy, a content and DM system that brings people to it, and a weekly routine that keeps it running.

Why I wrote this

I have spent 16 years in tech, a lot of it running programmes for large organisations, including at EY and Accenture. It took me close to six years to work out what I actually wanted to build.

When AI tools became good enough, I stopped waiting for a team. I built a temple-booking platform for Marudhamalai, a business-fit quiz with a paid 30-day course, and a wellness brand around South Indian food — mostly on weekends and evenings, mostly with Claude and ChatGPT doing the first draft of every job.

Some of it worked. A lot of it didn't. Across everything, I've made 57 paid sales so far: about 12 Murugaaa temple-visit bookings worth close to ₹50,000, 43 sales of a ₹99 offer, and 2 of a ₹499 course. That last number cost about ₹60,000 in ads. Mentell went through three websites before it had a paying customer. This book shows both sides, so you can skip the expensive parts.

— Noor

Meet Arjun

Arjun is you, roughly. Salaried, good at his job, curious about AI, no coding background, and about ten hours a week to spare once the family is fed. You'll see him at the start of each part — at his office desk in Part 1, at a café with a live product by Part 6.

When a chapter says "Arjun would…", it means: here's what a normal person with a job does at this step, not a full-time founder with a team.

chapters.title: Why AI changes the math for employees
chapters.promise: Building a product used to need a team and a budget. Now it needs a laptop, two AI assistants and your weekends.
chapters.html:
Five people, three months, one big bet

Until recently, a small online product needed a designer, a developer, a copywriter, someone to research the market and someone to run the numbers. Each of them cost money before you had a single customer.

For a salaried person, that made every idea a big bet. You had to be sure before you started — and nobody is sure before they start. So most good ideas stayed in a notes app, and the people who did launch were the ones who could afford to be wrong.

Insight

The problem was never your idea. It was the cost of finding out whether it worked.

The team you used to hire now fits in two browser tabs

You still do the thinking. AI does the first draft of each job. Here is how the six jobs split in my builds:

Job Who drafts it now What you still do
Researcher ChatGPT (web search, quick comparisons) Decide which findings are real
Copywriter ChatGPT for ideas, Claude for final pages Cut, correct, make it sound like you
Designer Canva + AI images Pick, reject, keep it consistent
Developer Claude (pages, scripts, fixes) Test on your phone, report what broke
Analyst Claude (reading your numbers, spotting leaks) Make the decision
Marketer AI drafts posts and DMs Post, reply, show your face

Chapter 6 shows how to choose between ChatGPT and Claude for each job. For now, notice the pattern: every row still has a human column. AI removed the cost of the first draft, not the need for judgement.

What actually changed

Three things changed at the same time:

  1. Drafts got cheap. A landing page, a 2,000-word guide, a pricing table, a Google Apps Script — each used to be days of someone's time. Now each is minutes of yours, plus review.
  2. Iteration got cheap. If version one is wrong, version two costs another ten minutes, not another invoice. That changes how you work: you test instead of plan.
  3. The tools talk to each other. Claude can read your Google Drive, write to GitHub, and design in Canva through connectors (Chapter 9). Copy-paste between twelve tools is mostly gone.

AI didn't make building free. It made finding out cheap enough to do on weekends.

Four jobs that stay yours

Be honest about this part, because most AI courses aren't.

  • Talking to customers. AI can write the questions. Only you can sit through the answers and notice what people avoid saying.
  • Taste. AI gives you ten options. Picking the right one, and knowing why the other nine are wrong, is the skill.
  • Trust. Buyers trust a person with a face, a name and a story — not a tool. Your credibility is the one asset AI can't generate.
  • Deciding. What to build, what to cut, when to stop. That's the founder's job, and it doesn't get easier with better models.
Mistake I made

I let AI-written strategy replace real conversations. I had polished plans for Mentell — positioning, pricing tiers, content calendars — and almost no conversations with people who might pay. From Chapter 12 on, every idea in this book gets five real conversations before anything is built.

In my build — murugaaa.in was built on ₹0 and broke even in month 5. Claude wrote most of the code. The temple visits, the conversations with devotees and the trust of the people running things locally made it work.

Action page

Action checklist

  • Open free accounts on ChatGPT and Claude
  • List 3 ideas you've sat on for more than a year
  • Block 2 weekend slots in your calendar for next weekend

Homework (under 60 minutes)

For one idea, write which of the six jobs it needs and which tool would draft each one.

Prompt exercise

Business exercise

Write down what testing this idea would have cost you five years ago, and what it costs this month.

Reflection

  • Which of the six jobs do you most want to avoid? Why?
  • What would you build if finding out cost almost nothing?
